common_name: Immortality Bearded Iris (Reblooming White Bearded Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun so roots establish before frost; as a heavy rebloomer, Immortality also benefits from a light feeding after its main spring flush to fuel the fall rebloom.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun — never bury them, since covered rhizomes are prone to iris borers and rot. Introduced in 1982 and still one of the most dependable and widely planted reblooming bearded iris, Immortality produces crisp, pure white ruffled flowers with a light fragrance in a strong late-spring flush, followed by a reliable second bloom in late summer or fall across a wide range of climates, including many areas too cold for most other rebloomers. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years after bloom, discarding the older woody center rhizome and replanting vigorous outer fans in well-drained soil. Good drainage is essential — soggy soil causes rhizome rot far more readily than drought stresses the plant.

common_name: Beverly Sills Bearded Iris (Award-Winning Coral-Pink Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil; soggy conditions cause rhizome rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought. Named for the opera singer and introduced in 1979, Beverly Sills is one of the most decorated bearded iris cultivars ever released, winning both the American Iris Society's Award of Merit and its top honor, the Dykes Medal, for its ruffled, coral-pink flowers with a bright tangerine beard on tall, well-branched stems. Its clear, luminous color and vigorous, floriferous habit have kept it a garden and show standard for decades. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting healthy outer fans.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil in full sun. Introduced in 1977, Superstition remains one of the darkest bearded iris ever bred, its huge, velvety flowers appearing nearly black-purple in the garden, especially in strong sun, with a subtle sheen that catches the light differently than true black. Its dramatic, almost theatrical color makes it a strong focal-point plant and a favorite for contrast plantings against silver or white companions. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting vigorous outer fans; good drainage is essential to prevent rhizome rot.

common_name: Stairway to Heaven Bearded Iris (Reblooming Blue-and-White Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; feed lightly after the spring bloom to support fall rebloom.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil in full sun. Stairway to Heaven is a dependable reblooming bearded iris with crisp white standards over rich medium-blue falls, each fall marked with a bright orange beard, producing a strong spring flush followed by reliable rebloom in late summer and fall in most climates. Its two-tone blue-and-white color combination and dependable second bloom have made it a favorite among rebloom-focused iris gardeners looking to extend the iris season well past the usual few spring weeks. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years after bloom, discarding the woody center and replanting vigorous outer fans in well-drained soil.

common_name: Victoria Falls Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal Light Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil in full sun. Introduced in 1977 and a Dykes Medal winner, Victoria Falls bears tall, elegant, clear light-blue flowers on strong, well-branched stems, with a form and substance that set a benchmark for blue bearded iris breeding for years afterward. Its clean, luminous color and vigorous, floriferous habit have kept it in wide cultivation long after many of its contemporaries faded from commerce. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years after bloom, discarding the older woody center rhizome and replanting healthy outer fans; good drainage is essential to prevent rot.

common_name: Café au Lait Dahlia (Blush Cream Dinner-Plate Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers 4–6 inches deep after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; stake tall plants at planting time since the huge blooms are heavy.

directions: Plant tubers 4–6 inches deep in full sun and rich, well-drained soil after frost, staking plants early since the enormous flowers are heavy on the stem. Café au Lait has become one of the most sought-after dinner-plate dahlias in cultivation, prized especially by wedding and cut-flower growers for its huge, 8–10 inch, softly ruffled flowers in shifting shades of creamy blush, dusty peach, and pale caramel that vary with temperature and light. Pinch the growing tip early to encourage branching, disbud side buds for the largest single blooms if exhibition-size flowers are the goal, and cut often to keep new flowers coming. In zones colder than 8, lift tubers after the first light frost blackens the foliage and store them in a cool, dry, frost-free place over winter.

common_name: Babylon Bronze Dahlia (Giant Copper-Bronze Dinner-Plate Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers 4–6 inches deep after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; stake tall plants at planting time since the giant blooms are heavy.

directions: Plant tubers 4–6 inches deep in full sun and rich, well-drained soil after frost, and stake plants at planting time since the massive flower heads weigh down the stems in wind and rain. Part of the Babylon series of giant dinner-plate dahlias, Babylon Bronze produces flowers up to 10 inches across in warm copper-bronze and burnt-orange tones that deepen toward the center, making a bold, dramatic statement in the back of a cutting garden or mixed border. Pinch the growing tip early to encourage a bushier, more floriferous plant, and disbud surrounding side buds if the largest possible single blooms are the goal. In zones colder than 8, lift tubers after the first light frost blackens the foliage and store in a cool, dry, frost-free place over winter.

planting.note: Plant tubers 4–6 inches deep after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; also does well started from seed for bedding use, since Fascination breeds fairly true.

directions: Plant tubers 4–6 inches deep in full sun and rich, well-drained soil after frost, spacing plants 12–18 inches apart for a compact bedding effect. An Award of Garden Merit winner, Fascination is a dwarf, bushy dahlia grown as much for its dark bronze-purple, finely cut foliage as for its semi-double, bright pink flowers with a lighter pink collar, produced prolifically from midsummer through frost. Its compact habit needs no staking and no pinching, making it far lower-maintenance than tall dinner-plate types, and its dark foliage adds season-long contrast in mixed containers and border edges even between flushes of bloom. In zones colder than 8, lift tubers after the first light frost blackens the foliage and store in a cool, dry, frost-free place over winter.

common_name: Gitts Perfection Dahlia (Formal Decorative Show Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers 4–6 inches deep after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; stake tall plants at planting time since the huge blooms are heavy.

directions: Plant tubers 4–6 inches deep in full sun and rich, well-drained soil after frost, staking plants early since the giant, formal blooms are heavy on the stem. A longtime favorite on the dahlia show bench, Gitts Perfection produces huge, perfectly formed, formal decorative blooms in soft lavender-pink with neatly overlapping, evenly spaced petals — the precise, symmetrical form that show judges look for in the formal decorative class. Pinch the growing tip early to build a well-branched plant, and disbud surrounding side buds to concentrate energy into fewer, larger, exhibition-quality blooms. In zones colder than 8, lift tubers after the first light frost blackens the foliage and store in a cool, dry, frost-free place over winter.

Ice Carnival is a long-popular near-white daylily, its ruffled, cream-white flowers with a faint chartreuse-green throat appearing about as close to true white as daylily breeding has achieved, blooming heavily over a long midseason display. Its pale flowers show up strikingly at dusk and under low light, making it a good choice near patios or evening seating areas. Divide overcrowded clumps every 4–5 years in early spring or late summer when bloom quality declines, and remove spent scapes after all buds open to keep the planting tidy.

Condilla is a compact, heavy-blooming daylily prized for its fully double, deep golden-yellow flowers that hold their ruffled, peony-like form reliably even in Gulf South heat and humidity, where many double daylily cultivars revert to single form. Its low, tidy habit and long midsummer bloom season suit it to border edges and mass plantings where reliable double flowers are wanted without fuss. Divide overcrowded clumps every 4–5 years in early spring or late summer when bloom quality declines.

Final Touch earns its name as one of the latest-blooming daylily cultivars widely grown, opening its ruffled, near-white flowers with a faint yellow-green throat well after most other daylilies have finished for the season, extending the daylily display into late summer. Planting it alongside early- and midseason cultivars stretches the overall daylily bloom season by several extra weeks in the garden. Divide overcrowded clumps every 4–5 years in early spring or late summer when bloom quality declines, and remove spent scapes after all buds open to keep the planting tidy.

Spider Miracle belongs to the spider class of daylilies, defined by petals at least four times longer than they are wide, producing dramatically narrow, twisting, lavender-purple petals with a lime-green throat that give each flower a starburst, spidery form very different from the rounder, more overlapping petals of classic daylily types. Its tall scapes and unusual flower form make it a strong textural contrast planted among rounder-flowered daylily cultivars. Divide overcrowded clumps every 4–5 years in early spring or late summer when bloom quality declines.

Buttered Popcorn is a classic, reliable, heavy-blooming daylily with rounded, ruffled, rich golden-yellow flowers with a lightly ruffled edge, produced in abundance over a long midseason bloom period on well-branched scapes with high bud count. Its dependable vigor, strong scapes, and clear, cheerful color have kept it a garden standard for mass plantings and mixed borders for decades. Divide overcrowded clumps every 4–5 years in early spring or late summer when bloom quality declines, and remove spent scapes after all buds open to keep the planting tidy.
